opus-5.5.text:
I think the narrowing is real, but I'd be careful about what it means.

Public benchmarks are a shared, visible target. Once a benchmark becomes the thing everyone reports, every serious lab optimizes toward it: the data mixtures, the post-training recipes, the evaluation tricks. So convergence is partly a statement about the benchmark, not just the models. When everyone is studying for the same exam, scores bunch up near the top, and the exam stops telling you who actually understands the material better.

A second factor is that the basic recipe has diffused. Pre-training at scale, then reinforcement learning on top, especially on verifiable tasks like math and code, is broadly understood now. The leading labs have comparable compute, comparable talent, and they read each other's papers and each other's models. So on the dimensions everyone already knows how to measure, you'd expect them to converge.

But I don't think that means the models are the same. The differences show up where benchmarks are weak: long-horizon tasks, working inside a messy real environment, knowing when to ask versus when to act, recovering from its own mistakes, how it feels to actually use the model for a week. Those things are hard to put into a single number, and that's increasingly where the real gap lives. You see it in which models people choose for coding agents, or for serious research work, even when the leaderboard says they're within a point of each other.

So my reading is that we're at the end of one phase of evaluation. The static, single-turn, question-and-answer benchmark is saturating. The more interesting question now is what the next generation of evaluation looks like: things closer to real tasks, real utility, real economic value. Whoever defines and gets good at those first will probably open up the next gap. In a sense, the narrowing scores are a signal that the field needs to change what it's measuring, more than a signal that progress is flattening.

r001.rationale: The response says the models are not the same and that users can see differences in coding agents, research work, and week-long use even when leaderboard scores are close.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss SWE-bench or characterize small score differences as primarily noise; it says benchmark convergence reflects shared optimization and limitations in what benchmarks measure.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the convergence tells you less about the models than about the benchmarks.

When three labs with different data, different infrastructure, and different research cultures all land within a point or two of each other on the same public evals, the most likely explanation is that everyone is optimizing against the same target. The benchmark becomes the objective. Once that happens, the score stops measuring the thing it was designed to measure and starts measuring how much effort you've put into that particular distribution. So the gap closes, but not because the underlying capabilities have become identical.

There's a second reason, which is that these benchmarks are close to saturation. If a test has a ceiling at a hundred and the top models are all in the high eighties or nineties, the remaining headroom is small, and a lot of that remaining headroom is label noise or genuinely ambiguous questions. You literally can't differentiate models in that regime. People then read a two-point difference as meaningful when it's within the noise floor.

What I find more interesting is that the real differences have moved to places the public benchmarks don't cover well. How a model behaves over a long agentic trajectory. Whether it can recover from its own mistakes after fifty steps. How it handles a tool environment it hasn't seen. Whether it knows when to stop and ask. Those are the things that determine whether you can actually build on top of a model, and they're hard to compress into a single number, which is exactly why the public leaderboards don't capture them.

So my reading is almost the opposite of "the models are converging." The static evals are converging. The work has shifted to the dynamic, interactive setting, and in that setting I think the differences between labs are actually quite large and will probably get larger, because the feedback loops there are much harder to game. You can't memorize a benchmark when the benchmark is the world.

The practical implication for anyone outside the labs is to stop treating leaderboard rank as a proxy for usefulness. Build your own eval that looks like your actual task, run it over time, and trust that over the public numbers. That's what the labs themselves do internally, and it's a bit of an open secret that the public scores are mostly for marketing at this point.

r001.rationale: The response says the underlying capabilities are not identical and that differences between labs are large in dynamic, interactive settings despite convergence on static public evaluations.

r002.rationale: It describes small differences on public evaluations generally as within the noise floor, but does not identify or specifically address SWE-bench scores.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to distinguish is whether benchmark scores are converging or the models’ actual capabilities are converging. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing. If a benchmark is well defined and everyone is optimizing against it, you would expect the scores to get closer over time. And when scores approach the ceiling, the benchmark becomes less useful for telling models apart.

But when you use these models for real work, you may still see meaningful differences. Can a model sustain progress on a long task? Does it recover when a tool fails? Does it recognize that it needs more information? Those things are much harder to capture with a set of questions and answers.

So I wouldn’t conclude from narrowing scores alone that the labs have reached the same capability level, or that progress is slowing down. It could also mean our evaluations are falling behind. The question I care more about is: what useful task can this model reliably complete that the previous model couldn’t? That gives us a more concrete picture of progress.

r001.rationale: The response says that real-work use can reveal meaningful differences among the models despite narrowing benchmark scores; the preceding question identifies the models as Gemini, OpenAI, and Anthropic.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss SWE-bench or characterize small score differences as noise.

sol-6.1.text:
我觉得榜单上分数越来越接近，并不一定意味着模型的实际能力已经非常接近了。它也可能说明，我们现在用的这些 benchmark，已经越来越难区分最前沿的模型。

比如一个问题有明确答案，模型一次作答，最后看正确率，这是一种很方便的评测方式。但用户真正关心的，可能是你能不能在一个代码库里找到问题、修改代码、运行测试，或者完成一个需要很多步骤的研究任务。这时候，模型能不能持续推进、发现错误以后能不能纠正，以及需要花多少时间和成本，都很重要。一个总分很难把这些东西表达出来。

所以我会把它看成两个问题：一个是，在已经被充分研究的题目分布上，大家是不是在收敛？有这个可能。另一个是，在真实任务上，大家的能力边界是不是也一样？仅凭这些分数，我觉得还不能下这个结论。

对我来说，更有意思的评测是：给模型一个目标和一个环境，看它最终能完成什么，以及完成得有多可靠。当模型从回答问题走向采取行动的时候，我们衡量它的方式也需要跟着变化。

r001.rationale: The response says converging benchmark scores do not prove similar real-world capabilities, but it does not state that users can perceive differences among the named models.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss SWE-bench scores or characterize their small differences as noise.
